subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
passage: Manjula, you say your junior writes down every word you say as if it were scripture. I had a junior like that when I was twenty-six, a young man named Ravi. I loved it, honestly. I also felt uneasy, because I knew my advice on client calls was mostly luck. One day he rewrote a whole quotation because I had "sounded sure," and it cost us the deal. I told him plainly that I had been guessing, and that I had made three mistakes myself that month. After that I began asking him, "What would you do? Why?" before I answered. He hated it at first. Later he started disagreeing with me, and I saw that admiration can either bind a person to you or help them stand up. Be careful which one you feed. Devika

qa.q: What did Ravi change because Devika sounded sure?
qa.a: He rewrote a whole quotation, and it cost the deal.

qa.q: Why did Devika feel uneasy about Ravi's admiration?
qa.a: Devika knew that the advice on client calls was mostly luck and did not deserve to be treated as gospel.

qa.q: What did Devika start doing to encourage independent thinking?
qa.a: Asking Ravi what he would do and why before giving an answer.

qa.q: How did Ravi react at first to being asked?
qa.a: He hated it at first but later began disagreeing, which shows growing independence.

grounding: An elder recalls a junior who treated every word as gospel, and how sharing mistakes and asking the junior to think built independence.

subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
passage: Rehana, you asked how to handle the new trainees who follow you around. Let me tell you about Tulsi. When I was twenty-five and a new ward sister, Tulsi joined as a trainee nurse and wrote down everything I said. Every word. If I said "always check the drip twice", she checked it four times. It felt lovely, I won't pretend otherwise. But one day she repeated a shortcut of mine to a doctor as if it were a rule, and it was wrong. My face went hot. That evening I told her about three mistakes I had made in my first year, including one that frightened me badly. I said, "Don't copy me. Ask why." After that I answered her questions with questions. Tulsi runs her own ward now. She argues with me at every reunion, and I'm proud of that. That was my lesson, Rehana, from your old Yamini-didi.

qa.q: What did Tulsi do with everything Yamini said?
qa.a: She wrote it down, every word.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when Tulsi repeated the wrong shortcut?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and uneasy, her face hot, realising Tulsi's admiration made her words carry too much weight.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Tulsi learned?
qa.a: Yamini shared three of her own early mistakes and began answering Tulsi's questions with questions, telling her to ask why.

qa.q: How might Tulsi have felt when Yamini shared her mistakes?
qa.a: Tulsi may have been surprised and a little shaken, but also relieved to learn that even a senior she admired had made mistakes.

grounding: An elder recalls a junior who treated her words as gospel; she felt flattered but uneasy, shared her mistakes, and encouraged independent thinking.

subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
passage:
It was 11 p.m. and the client deadline was at nine the next morning. Salma was checking the last slides when Anjali, her junior of four months, rolled her chair over again.
"Salma di, should the chart be blue or green? You'll know what's best."
It was the sixth time that evening. Anjali had started dressing like her, using her phrases in meetings, saying "Salma di says" before every opinion. Part of Salma liked it. Part of her felt a prickle of discomfort.
She pushed the laptop back. "Anju, I once lost a client because I chose a chart colour nobody could read on their projector. So don't trust me blindly. What do you think works, and why?"
Anjali hesitated. "Green. The logo's green."
"Good reason. Do it."
At midnight, packing up, Salma sent her a message: "Lead the chart review tomorrow. Your call on it. 🙂"

qa.q: What time was the client deadline?
How did Salma feel about Anjali copying her, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Salma felt flattered but uncomfortable; part of her liked it and part of her felt a prickle of discomfort.

qa.q: How did Salma encourage Anjali to think for herself?
qa.a: She shared a past mistake, asked Anjali for her own reasoning, and then asked her to lead the chart review the next day.

qa.q: What might Anjali be feeling when she hesitates before saying "Green"?
qa.a: Anjali may feel nervous and unsure, used to deferring to Salma, and then encouraged when her own reason is accepted.

grounding: A junior treats the protagonist's word as gospel; she feels flattered and uneasy, shares a mistake, and encourages the junior to decide for herself.
